title: Understanding fleece grades
subtitle: How fibre micron count, staple length, and vegetable matter affect what a fleece is worth and what it can be used for.
excerpt: The value and usefulness of a fleece depends on a handful of measurable qualities: the fineness of the individual fibres, the length of the staple, the degree of contamination with vegetable matter, and the condition of the fibre tips. Understanding these grades helps you select the right breeds for your goals, present fleeces well to buyers and small-scale processors, and understand why a Border Leicester fleece and a Merino fleece are not interchangeable.
sourceNotes: British Wool Marketing Board (BWMB), Wool Grading Standards (2023). The Campaign for Wool, Fibre Guides (2022). Phil Greenslade, British Wool Breed Descriptions (BWMB, 2021). John Linstrum, The Encyclopaedia of Fleece (reprint 2009), chapter on grading terms. National Sheep Association, British Sheep Breeds and their Wool (2022).

glossaryTerms.definition: The diameter of an individual wool fibre measured in micrometres (microns). Fine Merino runs below 22 microns; medium British breeds (Cheviot, Bluefaced Leicester) run 26 to 32 microns; coarse breeds (Scottish Blackface, Swaledale) run 33 microns and above. The micron count determines how soft a fibre feels against skin.
The length of a lock of wool from cut end to tip, measured after shearing. Spinning mills specify minimum staple length requirements; a short or irregular staple limits processing options.

Seeds, burrs, hay, and other plant material embedded in a fleece. VM must be removed before processing; at high levels it significantly reduces commercial value and is difficult to remove without damaging fibre.

content.text: A fleece is not one material: its specific properties determine what it can be made into and how to present it for sale or processing. The key properties are fibre fineness (
micron count
), staple length, vegetable matter content, and tip condition.
Micron count and end use
The
micron count

governs whether a wool feels soft or scratchy against skin. Fibres below about 22 microns are nearly universally described as next-to-skin soft. Above 30 microns they will itch against most people's bare skin, which does not make them inferior: coarser wools are stronger and better suited to floor rugs, bags, heavy outerwear, and felting projects where durability matters more than softness.
Below 22 microns: fine Merino, Rambouillet. Next-to-skin garments, fine lace, baby items.
22 to 26 microns: Corriedale, Polwarth, Bluefaced Leicester. Sweaters, socks, fine outerwear that may touch skin.
26 to 33 microns: most UK longwools (Border Leicester, Romney, Texel). Textured knitting yarn, weaving warps, upholstery.
Above 33 microns: Scottish Blackface, Herdwick, Swaledale. Tweed, rugs, felting. Not soft enough for skin contact in most people.
Staple length
The
staple length

reflects how long the sheep has been growing fleece since the last shear. UK commercial shearing is annual, producing a staple of 70 to 130 mm depending on breed. Spinning mills generally require a minimum of 50 to 70 mm for woollen-spun yarn and 60 to 80 mm for worsted. Short staples and broken staples (split part-way along the length due to stress or disease) are a significant downgrade.
Vegetable matter
High
vegetable matter

content is the most common reason a good fleece achieves a low commercial price. Hay-fed sheep in a barn over winter accumulate significant VM in the fleece. Sheep on grass with clean pasture management produce much cleaner fleeces. For smallholders selling to hand spinners or small processors, a clean, VM-free fleece commands a significant premium over British Wool Marketing Board grading prices.
Tip condition

The tip of the staple (the end that was furthest from the skin at shearing) can be weathered, sun-bleached, discoloured, or matted. Discoloured tips are cut off in processing but represent waste fibre. A fleece with matted or heavily weathered tips is processed with a yield penalty.
British Wool Marketing Board grading

In the UK most commercial fleeces pass through the British Wool Marketing Board (BWMB), which grades them on a series of codes (e.g. Fine White, Medium White, Coarse White, Hog, various coloured grades). The BWMB publishes grade specification cards that define exactly what each grade accepts and rejects. If you are registered with the BWMB and selling through their system, presenting clean, dry, well-rolled fleeces is the main variable you control.

Smallholders with rare breed, coloured, or fine-fibre fleeces often achieve better returns by selling directly to hand spinners, small dyers, and indie yarn producers rather than through the BWMB commodity route. Direct buyers typically pay significantly more per kilo for clean, well-presented fleeces of interesting breeds.
